Cargo nets hung from support beams overhead. Work lights dangled from cables stretched across the ceiling, casting pools of yellow light that never quite reached the corners. The place smelled strongly of saltwater, machine oil, damp wood, and old rope. It reminded me of every dockside storage facility I'd ever visited, which was probably intentional. Places used for smuggling generally benefited from looking exactly like places used for legitimate business.

There were perhaps a dozen people inside.

Most of them were older. Not elderly, but old enough that decades of physical labor had left visible marks. Their faces were weathered by wind and sea air. Their hands looked like they'd spent entire careers hauling cargo, repairing equipment, and solving problems that couldn't be fixed with a software update. A few looked up when we entered. Their eyes lingered on Vesper and me for a moment before returning to whatever they had been doing. Nobody looked alarmed. Nobody seemed particularly interested.

"You two can stay here for now," Solace said, drawing my attention back to the present. She spoke casually, as though she were offering directions rather than arranging an illegal escape. "The next boat we can smuggle you out on won't be here until much later tonight."

Vesper shifted her weight slightly as if she couldn't decide if she wanted to stay or run. Eventually, she gave in. "Okay." She inclined her head slightly. "Thank you for your assistance." The way she said thank you made it seem like it had pained her to say it.

"Asten!" Solace called, "Can you bring some food for our guests?"

A boy scrambled into view carrying a small box. He held it out to me and when i looked inside, there were a few apples.

publish_meta.summary:
Vesper, is a cybernetically enhanced mercenary trying to pay off crushing debt while searching for answers about her missing brothers. During what should be a routine theft, she steals a mysterious serum called Project Archangel and discovers that her experimental AI-assisted armor is beginning to override her free will.

At the same time, Hamish, a mage working as a mercenary, is sent to investigate a series of abandoned towns. What he finds is far worse than anyone expected: a spreading techno-organic plague that twists people, machines, and cybernetics into something monstrous.
When powerful forces place a bounty on Hamish and begin hunting anyone connected to the outbreak, Vesper and Hamish are forced into an uneasy partnership. Together they must uncover the truth behind Project Archangel

body.title: Prologue
body.content:
Artem Karpov

I clung to the shadows in this dimly lit corner, the cold rim of the shot glass pressed against my lips. The burn of the whiskey barely registered, my knuckles white from gripping the glass too tightly.

Across the room, the bride and groom moved together on the dance floor. Their movements almost dreamlike. Each beat from the speakers thudded in my chest, the sound was taunting. It was a relentless reminder of everything that had happened.

I felt my jaw tighten while I watched them. The swirl of her dress. The way his hand rested against her waist. I should’ve looked away. I wanted to. The urge twisted in my gut, but my eyes wouldn’t obey. I couldn’t tear myself from the scene, from the betrayal dancing before me. Each step they took was another knife, twisting deeper.

I prayed fervently to any god that might be listening to build this betrayal into an armor that I’d wear around my broken heart. Allow the mask I was supposed to wear slide back into place.

My chest felt tight. And for a brief moment I imagined I was having a heart attack the way it felt. I snorted slightly. Wouldn’t that just ruin the happy evening?

I threw back the last of the drink, the liquid fire scorching its way down my throat, but it did nothing to dull the ache. The walls and the party felt like they were closing in, the air too thick to breathe. I pushed up from the table, the need to escape it all clawing at me.

Slipping through the crowd like a ghost, unnoticed in the sea of celebration. I wiped at the corner of my eyes with my sleeve, my breath catching in my throat. No one even spared a glance in my direction.

I would think someone might pause, might question the best man tearing up at his friend’s wedding, but laughter and music drowned out the cracks in my composure.

I shoved the balcony doors open, the crisp autumn air slapping against my face, sharp and unforgiving. It It grounded me for a moment bringing me back.

I stared out into the night, the cold metal of the railing biting into my palms. I wasn’t just any man—I was about to take the reins of one of the largest corporations in the state.

Yet here I was, rattled by a wedding, of all things.

Emotion wasn’t normally built into us. Trained out of us by our fathers at a young age. Yet my grip on it was slipping. I was struggling to keep the mask of self-control intact.

The soft creak of the doors behind me broke through my thoughts. I didn’t have to turn around to know who it was—the familiar sound of the footsteps of none other than the groom himself.

“Did you come here to rub this victory of yours in my face?” I asked, my voice rough with bitterness, turning to face him. He stood there with a cocky smirk, his gray three-piece suit looking pricey—probably as damn expensive as this lavish country mansion they had booked. Hell, for all I know, he owned the place.

I pulled a cigar from my pocket and brought it to my lips, rolling it between my fingers, but I didn’t bother lighting it. The taste of tobacco lingered, offering a small distraction.

He grinned, that easy smile of his never faltering. “No, I came here to escape the chaos,” he said, leaning casually against the railing. “Figured I’d find some peace with my best friend.”

“Won’t the guests miss you?” I spat, each word thick with disdain. Fuck, how I wanted to strangle him.

He shrugged, his fingers coolly adjusting his cuff links, as if the weight of his answer was nothing. “I think my wife can handle that,” he said, his tone maddeningly calm.

That was it. The dam broke.

“Your wife!” The words tore from me, hot and raw. “Are you fucking serious? A week ago, Angela was my girlfriend, and now you’re fuckin’ married to her!” My voice echoed out. My heart ached with the effort of trying to keep it all contained. “How could you do that to me?”

He raised a single brow at my outburst as he closed the space between us. His face was an unreadable mask, but his eyes held something darker. “Careful, brother,” he said, his voice a low, dangerous growl. The way he said ‘brother’ mocked me. It cut deeper than the word itself.

But I didn’t care. The anger inside me surged, too hot to hold back. “How could you betray me like this?” I roared again, my fists trembling at my sides, the cold air doing nothing to cool the fire burning inside me.

He didn’t flinch. Instead, he met my fury with contempt, his lips curling into another smirk. “The real question is, how could you let your heart be swayed by something as weak as love?” His voice was laced with disdain, each word felt like a dagger aimed at my chest.

“You were my friend,” I said, my voice cracking. Disbelief and betrayal choked the words as they slipped past my lips. They trembled, like the rest of me, the weight of the truth too much to bear.

He smiled, placing a firm hand on my shoulder, his eyes gleaming with something dark and calculating. “I can still be your friend,” he said smoothly, a brief twinkle in his eye that didn’t reach his voice. “All you have to do is put this bullshit aside, and we can move on.”

He tugged me closer, his grip tightened just enough to discourage any reaction. His intent was clear. “Together, with her father’s money behind us, we could rule this city. Kings of Queens,” he whispered, his voice a velvet promise. “Just forget all this unpleasantness and focus on the future. Think about the power we could have, the empire we could build.”

His words hung in the air, dripping with temptation. The offer was seductive—almost too good to refuse. But as I stared at him disbelief flickered through my shock. How could he think I could ever overlook the betrayal, the knife he’d driven into my back?

I shrugged his hand off my shoulder, my chest tightening with every shallow, strained breath. “I loved her,” I snapped, the words scraping out of my dry throat. My voice was rough and brittle, shattering under the weight of the anger and ache clawing inside me. “You knew that. I told you everything, trusted you with it, and you still took her from me.”

My hands trembled, fingers clenching and unclenching as I struggled to keep control. My voice rose, straining against the anger building inside me. “How am I supposed to look at you and feel anything but this?” The words spilled out, each one biting. “You tore down everything we built—no kings, no empire.” I took a step closer, my fists tightening as the bitterness twisted inside me like a knife. “You never cared about that, though. All you wanted was me, bound at your side, obeying without question.” The last words slipped out in a raw, uneven whisper, broken beyond repair.

“Would that be so bad?” His voice was smooth, barely above a murmur. A faint smirk tugged at the corner of his lips, his eyes gleaming with something unreadable, untouched by my anger. Amusement flickered in his gaze, my words slipping off him, dismissed as easily as water rolling off stone.

A sigh slipped from my lips, sinking into my chest like a stone. I should’ve seen it coming. My gaze dropped, barely lifting as I asked, “Do you even love her?” The question lingered in the air, hollow, the answer already etched into the silence long before I spoke.

He gave a careless shrug, his gaze icy, detached. “Does it matter?” he said, his tone casual, almost bored. “She serves her purpose.” A faint smirk tugged at his lips as he glanced away. “And if she’s fallen for me, well—that’s just icing on the cake.”

The words slipped out, barely louder than the hum of the city below. Faint music drifted from inside, mingling with the distant sounds of laughter and clinking glasses. But I caught his words, and that unguarded remark stung more than anything he’d thrown at me before.

It wasn’t a surprise, not really—I had known from the start that Angela’s heart had never truly been mine, only resting with me as a second choice. When George finally turned his gaze toward her, she hadn’t even paused. She walked away without a glance. I’d been nothing more than a placeholder.

“You make me sick,” I snarled, the bitterness of the words burning on my tongue.

George didn’t flinch; his eyes gleamed with an unsettling calm as a smirk crept across his face. “Pity,” he murmured, his tone smooth, laced with a quiet menace. “This would be a good moment to reconsider.” He leaned in, his voice dropping, each word dripping with threat. “I’m wrapping this city around my finger. Trust me, you don’t want to be on the wrong side when that happens.”

I held his gaze, unmoved, letting his attempt at intimidation wash over me like a faint breeze. George could play at being powerful, but I knew him better than anyone—and I knew where to hit.

“You don’t scare me, George,” I said slowly. Carefully. “I know every secret you think you’ve buried.” I let the threat hang in the air, then turned away. “This is a debt,” I called over my shoulder, my tone calm, chilling. “And when I come to collect, you’ll pay every last bit.”

body.title: Lukas
body.content:
Thunder rumbled overhead, echoing down the sterile, empty hallways as I walked through the dimly lit corridors. Each step seemed to reverberate in the quiet, amplifying the isolation that clung to this place after hours. The overhead lights flickered, a brief pulse of uncertainty, but I barely registered it. Power outages in a corporate fortress like this were rare but not unheard of, and I had bigger concerns than worrying about losing a little light.

Every office I passed was shrouded in darkness, the typical employees long gone, eager to escape the confines of their cubicles for whatever waited for them beyond these walls. I didn’t blame them. In fact, if things had gone my way, I’d be at home right now, probably nursing a drink and sinking into my own familiar silence.

But fate—or rather, a late-night call—had other plans, dragging me back from the brink of freedom just as I was about to escape. Now, I was here, pacing empty corridors and feeling the oppressive weight of responsibility pressing down.

Every so often, a stray light would spill from an office door left ajar, casting a pale glow onto the floor. Probably some over-eager fool, convinced that staying late would impress the higher-ups, maybe even secure them a promotion. As if dedication could buy loyalty here.

The thought made me scoff under my breath. I knew better than most that loyalty was a fickle thing in this place, bought and sold like any other commodity. Those poor souls didn’t realize yet that working late only left them more vulnerable—more exposed to the shadows that prowled these halls after dark.

I came to a stop in the entryway to the departments reception area, leaning casually against the door frame like I owned the place—because, in a way, I did.

I watched the secretary, letting her feel the weight of my gaze before I made myself known. She was a pretty young thing, all long blonde hair and wide, innocent blue eyes. A little too eager, maybe, but that didn’t hurt her charm. Her skirt didn’t quite cover those long, slender legs, and she had the kind of look that made men do stupid things. The type they should’ve known better than to trust.

She noticed me only after a beat, and I caught the flicker of panic before she quickly straightened, her cheeks blooming with a shade of pink that betrayed her. She adjusted her collar, fingers fumbling ever so slightly as she tried to pull herself together.

“Oh, Mr. Karpov,” she stammered, her voice reaching for professionalism but betraying a tremble that told me all I needed to know. “I… I didn’t see you there.” She swallowed, casting a glance at the top of her desk before looking back up at me. “How long have you been waiting?”

I let the silence hang for a beat, watching her squirm before I finally shrugged, pushing off the door frame and striding toward her with deliberate ease, hands in my pockets, a hint of a smirk teasing at my lips. “Not long,” I replied, my gaze shifting to the heavy, oak double doors across the room. “He’s waiting for me?”

She followed my gaze, then flicked a quick, nervous look at the clock. Then bit her lower lip. “Yes, he’s… he’s in there. He was expecting you twenty minutes ago,” she said, her voice barely above a whisper. As if she didn’t want to rile up the man behind those doors by speaking too loudly. “You know he doesn’t like being kept waiting.”

I chuckled, the sound low and rough. I leaned in, arms folding across my chest as I fixed her with a knowing look. “Waiting won’t kill him,” I drawled, the words coming out as if I were savoring them. “I’m doing him a favor—keeping him on his toes.”

I pushed open one of the oak doors, the heavy wood creaking as if to announce my arrival. I didn’t bother to knock; why should I? If he was expecting me, he’d know I’d come when I felt like it.

“You’re late.” The words hit me like a cold gust of wind, his voice devoid of warmth, carrying the clipped edge of reprimand. Not even a glance in my direction—just a steady, unwavering gaze on the stack of paperwork in front of him.

“Nice to see you too, Father,” I replied, letting the sarcasm drip from my voice as I strolled over to the leather couch across from his desk. I sank down, lounging back as if I owned the place, one arm sprawled over the backrest, the other propping my head up.

My gaze flickered around his meticulously organized office, noting every polished surface, every neatly aligned pen, each detail reminding me just how little I belonged here.

Finally, he looked up, his piercing eyes narrowing as they took me in. Even at his age, Artem Karpov cut an imposing figure. The one thing we shared as father and son.

His jaw tightened slightly, a tell I’d learned to recognize over the years. He raised a brow, the look in his eyes equal parts disappointment and scrutiny. “Why are you late?” he asked, each word as sharp as a knife. “I called you over an hour ago.”

I shrugged, a lazy smirk tugging at the corner of my mouth. “I’ve got half a dozen excuses,” I drawled, meeting his stare with casual defiance. “None of them true, of course—so which one do you want to hear?”

“None of them,” he snapped, the sharpness in his voice like the crack of a whip. His gaze hardened, a look that brooked no patience for my games. “We have more pressing matters to attend to.” Without waiting for a response, he picked up a report from his desk.

“Care to explain,” he said, holding the paper up as if it were evidence in a trial, “how we’ve lost not only two weapon shipments but also an entire shipment of product?”

I fought the urge to roll my eyes, biting back a groan that threatened to escape. Of course, he wanted to talk about work. It was always work with him. And naturally, this was somehow my fault, even if I hadn’t heard a whisper about it until now. I shifted in my seat, feigning interest.

“I don’t know,” I replied, doing my best to sound as unruffled as possible. “This is the first I’m hearing of this.”

“Lukas,” my father said, his voice low and edged with cold authority. “This isn’t a game. We’ve been hemorrhaging money for months. Someone’s bleeding us dry from the inside, and we need to find the leak—or leaks—and plug it. Permanently.”

“You mean I have to fix it,” I shot back, matching his glare. “Because that’s what you always have me do, isn’t it? Clean up the mess, play the enforcer, take care of our problems.”

He didn’t flinch, his gaze as unyielding as granite, eyes narrowed with that familiar mix of disappointment and expectation. “It’s what you do best,” he said, his voice smooth but laced with a hint of venom.

I clenched my jaw, a retort forming on the tip of my tongue, but the sharp clamor of voices from down the hall cut through the tension like a blade. A muffled shout, then the thud of footsteps, heavy and hurried. The unmistakable sound of a struggle followed, curses from our security as they tried—and failed—to halt whoever was coming through.

The footsteps echoing down the hallway, getting closer—too close. A surge of adrenaline spiked through me, tightening every nerve as I shifted forward, now perched on the edge of the couch, ready.

My father’s gaze flickered briefly with something—recognition, maybe, though it was gone as quickly as it appeared. As the footsteps drew closer, his expression hardened, settling into that familiar mask of control. Without a word, he pulled open a drawer, his hand slipping inside and closing around the gun I knew he kept there.

The voices outside the office rose in pitch, tense and urgent, breaking through the silence like shattered glass. I caught fragments of shouting.

“Stop right there!”

“One more step, and we will fire!”

The guards were throwing everything they had into holding him back, their shouts edged with desperation. Whoever was coming wasn’t just pushing boundaries—they were bulldozing right through them.

I rose from the couch in one fluid motion, instincts honed by years in this life kicking in. My hand slipped to my side, drawing my gun in sync with my father, the metallic weight settling firmly in my grip. We both aimed at the doors, and waited.

Finally, the doors burst open, slamming against the walls with a force that rattled the frames. A man I didn’t recognize strode in. He held a gun, owning the room as if he’d been here a thousand times. His face—once, maybe, the kind that would’ve turned heads—looked like it had been battered by a lifetime of storms, lines etched deep into his skin. Dark hair streaked with gray framed piercing green eyes, sharp and cold.

He smirked at my father, the expression twisted by a jagged scar that carved from his jaw to just beneath his left eye. It gave his face a perpetual sneer, a hint of malice that seemed almost natural. “Glad to see we’re still on the same wavelength, Artem,” he drawled, his gaze flicking between us, amusement dancing in his eyes and threading through his voice.

“Take another step,” my father growled, the words low and edged with steel as he leveled the gun squarely at the stranger, his finger just grazing the trigger. “And I’ll put a fucking bullet in your chest.”

The stranger didn’t flinch at my father’s threat; in fact, he smirked, a dark glint in his eye that showed just how little he thought of it. He took a step forward and reached out, laying his hand on top of the gun. Then pressed it down, slow and controlled, like he already owned every soul in the room.

A flicker of anger flared up inside me, stoked by his audacity—the way he waltzed in here, casting aside my father’s authority like it was nothing.

I lunged forward, ready to grab his arm, to show him exactly who he was dealing with. But before my fingers brushed his sleeve, he moved. Swift as a viper, his hand shot out, clamping down on my wrist with a grip that was iron and ice, twisting my arm with brutal efficiency. Pain seared up through my shoulder as the gun slipped from my grasp, clattering to the floor.

“Now that we’ve all put our weapons down, maybe we can talk like men.” The stranger’s voice was smooth, a mocking edge lacing his words as he released my arm with a slight push, forcing me to take a step back.

I glared at him, rubbing my arm, the dull ache a reminder of his grip. He looked at me with an amused glint in his eye, daring me to make another move.

He sank onto the couch as if he owned it, one arm draped casually over the back, claiming space that wasn’t his to take. His other hand rested on his thigh, where his gun now rested. His legs were spread wide, posture loose, exuding a self-assurance that bordered on insolence. The arrogance radiated off him in waves, every inch of his relaxed sprawl a deliberate taunt.

“Unless you’re offering your head on a silver platter…” my father’s voice was sharp. “I’ll pass.” His gaze was steady, unblinking, a deadly calm radiating from him as he leveled his words at the intruder.

The stranger let out a derisive snort, a twisted smile tugging at his scarred face. “Come now, Artem, it’s been twenty five years. You still can’t be holding on to that?” His tone was a mocking drawl, like he found the whole thing amusing, as if time had dulled whatever sharp edge once lay between them.

“Who the hell are you?” I demanded, narrowing my eyes, studying him for any sign of recognition. His gaze flicked to me, briefly amused, as if I were an insect he’d decided to tolerate—for now.

“Artem, tell your boy to shut up and remember his place,” he said, turning his attention back to my father, his smirk widening.

“No,” my father replied coldly, “You barge in here, uninvited, acting like you call the shots. And we’re supposed to just sit back and listen?”

“Yes.” He said, grinning.

A surge of fury rose in me, the simple answer causing a wild heat igniting under my skin as anger bloomed hot and fast. Blurring the edges of my vision in a crimson haze. I could almost feel my pulse throbbing in my temples, fists itching to slam into the stranger’s smirking face. I took a step forward, ready to grab him by the collar. Then drag him out and feel the satisfaction of shutting him up with a well-placed punch.

But then my father’s gaze cut through the haze, cold and commanding—a silent warning that froze me mid-step.

“Lukas,” he said. His voice a low growl, laced with steel. “Control.”

The stranger’s smirk grew sharper, his gaze flicking to me with a mocking glint, eyes narrowed in a look of condescending amusement that made my blood boil. “That’s right,” he sneered, each word dripping with a poisonous taunt. “Be a good boy and sit.”

That was it.

My self-control snapped. I drew my fist back and drove it into his jaw. The impact sending a satisfying jolt through my arm as his head snapped to the side. His whole body rocked back on the couch.

“You little bastard,” the stranger growled, rubbing his jaw as he glared at me with a dark, seething intensity. He rose to his feet, and the next instant we were face to face.

“George,” my father snapped, his tone cutting through the tension like a blade. “Enough. You have sixty seconds to say what you came to say.”

“You’re going to listen to him after that?” I protested, my voice rising in disbelief. “He was—”

“Sit down and shut up for a moment,” my father interrupted, his glare turning on me, silencing any retort that was left on my tongue.

I swallowed hard, then grudgingly closed my mouth and dropped onto the edge of the couch, as far from George as possible. In the brief silence that followed, I could hear the muffled sounds of the thunderstorm outside.

“Now,” my father said, his voice low and unforgiving as he turned his attention back to George. “Sixty seconds.”

“Look,” George began, his tone taking on an edge of urgency. “The world we built our empires in—it’s changing, fast.” He paused, shaking his head as if to clear the thought. “There are new players in the game, ones who don’t respect the rules. They’re already making moves, power grabs. Seeing if we’ll slip up.”

“Forty seconds,” my father intoned, his voice flat, unimpressed, as if George’s presence was nothing more than a minor inconvenience.

George’s gaze hardened, a flicker of annoyance behind his eyes as he leaned in, his voice dropping to a low, threatening murmur. “You and yours could end up on the wrong side of this,” he warned. “I’m here to make sure that doesn’t happen.”

“Bullshit,” I muttered under my breath my voice thick with contempt. Men like him didn’t care about others; they only cared about what suited them.

My father seemed to share the sentiment, his expression carved from stone. He leveled George with a hard stare, eyes narrowed, scrutinizing him like something he found under his shoe. “Since when do you give a damn about my family?” he asked, his voice filled with disbelief. Then, after a beat, he added, “Twenty seconds.”

“Look, you’ve had some missing shipments recently, haven’t you? What was it? A weapons and a drug shipment?” George said, spreading his hands in a mock display of sincerity, his tone slipping into something almost pleading. “Me too. In the last six months I’ve lost thousands if not millions. We’re on the same side here. If we don’t join forces, we’ll both lose everything we’ve built.”

My father’s brows knit together, suspicion flashing in his eyes as he leaned back, arms crossing over his chest. A bitter laugh escaped his lips. “Join forces?” he echoed. “You must be out of your mind.” His gaze narrowed, sharp as a knife, cutting through George’s charade. “And exactly how do you plan to make that happen?”

“A truce,” George repeated, his voice hard and unyielding, but there—a flicker, barely noticeable, something almost vulnerable hiding beneath his stony exterior. Desperation, maybe. “We show a united front, and together, we’re untouchable.”

I held his gaze, finally breaking my silence, letting the weight of my words hit like a blow. “How?” I asked, my tone cold, distrust in every syllable. “And why the hell should we trust you?”

George’s jaw tightened, his eyes darkening as he registered my challenge. Whatever he’d expected, it wasn’t that, and for a second, he looked like a man cornered, fighting to keep his last card close to his chest.

“Answer him, George.” My father’s tone was cold, each word clipped and precise. He leaned back, eyes narrowing, studying George like he was dissecting a puzzle with missing pieces. “There’s more to this than you’re letting on.”

George hesitated, his jaw tightening as if he were biting back something bitter. Finally, he met our stares, his voice steady, but a shadow of reluctance in his eyes. “A marriage deal,” he said, each word heavy with intent. “That’s my offer.”

I blinked, twisting a finger in my ear as if I could somehow clear the shock clogging my brain. “Sorry, what was that?” I said, my voice thick with disbelief. “Did you just say… marriage?”

Beside me, my father’s eyebrows lifted, though he kept his composure, the barest hint of intrigue breaking through his usual stoic mask. “That’s an interesting offer.”

George’s mouth tightened, a flash of irritation crossing his face as he crossed his arms, his stance turning rigid. “Drop the theatrical bullshit,” he growled, his voice sharp, cutting through our reactions. “You heard me.”

My father let out a short, bitter laugh. A sound that held no humor, only scorn. He leaned back, his fingers loosening around his gun before he finally set it down on the table with a metallic clink that echoed through the tense silence. “Who, exactly, are you trying to shackle together in this twisted union?”

George’s gaze didn’t waver. “My daughter and your son.” He spoke as if it were the most logical thing in the world, as if marrying off our blood would somehow solve decades of bad blood. “They’re both of age, and as far as I know, both are single.” His lips curled into a smirk, his eyes flicking over to me with a pointed gleam. “Unless, of course, your promiscuous son has finally decided to settle down?”

I glared at him, my jaw clenched so tightly I thought my teeth might shatter. “Marriage? I don’t think I want anything to do with it.”

The idea of being tied down, of letting someone in close enough to see every flaw, every scar—it feels like a prison sentence. I can barely stand my own reflection most days; how could I expect someone else to bear it?

George didn’t even glance my way. “The adults are talking,” he snapped, his tone dismissive, as if I were nothing more than a buzzing fly to be ignored. He turned back to my father, his voice lowering into a harsh whisper. “Are you really that blind? You know as well as I do that this alliance is our best shot at survival.”

A hot surge of anger shot through me, making my fists clench so hard my knuckles went white. Every dismissive word hit me like a punch, each one chipping away at whatever restraint I had left. How could he talk about my life, my future, like it was some simple business transaction? Just another move on a chessboard, with me as a piece he could shove wherever he pleased.

“Excuse me,” I said, my voice sharp, nearly cracking with barely contained rage. I leaned forward, my eyes blazing. “I’m not a child. And I’m certainly not some pawn you can shove into place just because it suits your plans. You think you can control every aspect of my life-”

But my father raised a hand, cutting off my rant, gaze turning to me with that familiar, impenetrable hardness. “Lukas,” he commanded, his voice low and cold, like the snap of a trap shutting tight. “Wait outside.”

The protest rose in my throat, fierce and unyielding, but the look in his eyes stopped me short. That look—the one that had silenced me so many times, the one that warned there was no point in arguing. Not here, not now.

I threw one last searing glare at George before turning on my heel, each step heavy with the weight of my own anger and frustration. As I walked away, shoulders rigid, I could feel their gazes lingering, dismissive and calculating. Behind me, the door clicked shut, sealing off the murmur of their voices.

body.title: Lukas
body.content:
My footsteps thudded against the worn wood of the dimly lit hallway, the oppressive silence broken only by the occasional creak beneath my weight. At the far end, the metal door loomed, the faint sounds of hollow screams leaking through the cracks. I pushed it open slowly, the groaning hinges blending with the muffled cries inside.

The door clicked shut behind me, sealing the room in its own twisted, suffocating atmosphere. My eyes swept the scene, taking in the familiar sight. Mikhail had Jacob pinned to the chair, the man’s head slumped forward, sweat dripping from his brow in steady rivulets. His wrists were bound tightly to the arms of the chair, rope digging into flesh, the weight of his exhaustion clear.

For a fleeting moment, guilt twisted in my chest. But it passed quickly, fading like smoke as I remembered why we were here—why Jacob had earned this. Traitors were the worst kind of filth, and Jacob had sealed his own fate the moment he thought he could double-cross us.

Sandy sidled up beside me, his voice barely a whisper. “We caught him at the Emporium Hotel.”

I sighed, shaking my head. The Emporium—of course. That hole was a breeding ground for rats, for those who thought they could play both sides and come out on top. Traitors flocked there like moths to a flame, and Jacob was no different.

“You picked the wrong family to screw over, Jacob,” I said, my voice low, almost bored, as I stepped closer. I stopped in front of him, just out of reach, my gaze sweeping over his bruised and sweat-slicked face. His eyes fluttered open, meeting mine for just a second, wide and filled with fear. His breath hitched, a silent plea hiding behind that fear, but there would be no mercy here. Not tonight.

The room was heavy with the scent of sweat, blood, and fear—a cocktail that clung to the walls like a second skin. Jacob had been here for hours, under Mikhail’s relentless care, the tools of persuasion laid out neatly on the table nearby. The knives, the pliers, the lengths of cord—they were a silent reminder of the price of betrayal.

I took my time, letting the silence stretch between us, the weight of it pressing down. My gaze flickered to the table, and I picked up one of the knives, turning it over in my hand, feeling the cold weight of the steel. Its edge glinted under the dim light, a sliver of sharpness against the shadows. I held it up, watching the way Jacob’s eyes followed the blade, his pulse quickening in his throat.

Jacob’s breath came in ragged, uneven gasps, his lips parting as if to speak. But with a sharp flick of my wrist, I silenced him, the knife still dancing in my hand, catching the dull light. “You thought you could betray us and walk away clean?” My voice dropped to a low, menacing growl as I leaned in closer, the steel of the blade gleaming between us. “You have no idea what you’ve started. This… this is just the beginning.”

“P-please…” Jacob stammered, gasping between every breath. “I would n-never…”

The knife twirled in my fingers, a smooth, practiced motion that drew his wide, terrified eyes. His gaze stayed locked on it, following every rotation, each flick of my wrist. His body trembled, and I could see the fear taking root, paralyzing him.

“That’s what they all say,” Sandy muttered from behind, his voice dripping with disdain.

Jacob’s eyes darted toward Sandy for a brief moment, but before he could even think of responding, I stepped forward, placing my hand firmly against the wall behind the chair, my face just inches from his. His breath was hot and desperate on my cheek. The knife in my hand found its mark, sinking into the back of the chair just centimeters from his throat. The wood cracked and splintered under the force, the sound sharp in the tense silence.

“What did you do, Jacob?” My words were cold, biting, as I stared him down. I could practically see the gears turning in his head, the frantic calculations as he searched for a lie, something that might save his skin.

But before he could speak, I raised my hand, cutting him off before the falsehood even left his lips. “Don’t even think about lying to me,” I growled, my patience wearing thin.

Jacob swallowed hard, his Adam’s apple bobbing in his throat. Sandy stepped forward, handing me a thin folder. I flipped it open, revealing a set of photographs—grainy images of Jacob in a dimly lit alley, speaking with a tall, striking woman. I picked one up, turning it so that Jacob could see it clearly.

“I’m going to ask nicely one more time,” I said, my voice calm, though fury roiled beneath the surface. I recognized her, and the very thought of her sent a spike of rage through me.

Jacob’s eyes widened as he took in the photo, panic flickering behind his gaze. “I-I met a w-woman,” he stammered, his voice trembling. “She p-promised that if I j-just gave her a little information on you, we could b-be together.”

For a brief moment, pity flickered through me. He was a fool, easily manipulated. But that pity quickly morphed into disgust. “You were played, Jacob,” I said, my voice hardening. “She played you like a violin, and you let her. Hook, line, and sinker.”

Jacob’s face contorted with confusion, his lips trembling. “W-what do you mean?”

I tapped the photograph with the back of the knife. “That woman? She’s not who you think she is. That’s Carpathia’s Widow Maker.” I leaned in closer, my voice dropping to a whisper. “Her real name is Natalie Drayton. She’s as deadly as she is beautiful.”

The shock on Jacob’s face was almost laughable. “N-no! You’re wrong!”

I shook my head, my tone mocking. “Think about it. She was going to milk you for every scrap of information she could get. And once you were no longer useful?” I paused, letting the weight of my words sink in. “She was going to kill you.”

Jacob’s body trembled, his face pale as the realization dawned on him. He looked away, unable to meet my gaze any longer, the denial still clinging to him like a desperate hope.

I straightened, stepping back as the weight of the moment settled over the room. I cast a glance at Sandy, who stood ready. “Get every piece of information out of him. I want to know exactly what he told Natalie. Then…” My eyes flicked back to Jacob’s trembling form. “Finish him. Leave his body at the Emporium. Let them see what happens when you cross us.”

Sandy gave a sharp nod, stepping aside as I made my way to the door. Jacob’s pleas, his desperate cries for mercy, rang out behind me, growing more frantic with every step I took. But I didn’t stop.

Mercy had no place here. Not today.

***

My fingers dug into the chipped paint of the door frame, the rough edges biting into my skin as I clung to it, my knuckles white. I couldn’t stop the tears. They streamed down my face, hot and relentless, blurring my vision.

My body trembled uncontrollably as I pressed myself against the wall, straining to stay hidden, listening to the shouting from the other room.

“I didn’t want this!” my mother’s voice cut through the air, sharp and high-pitched, each word like a jagged knife. “I never wanted any of this, or your baggage!”

My breath hitched in my throat. My father’s reply came, low and cold, with an edge that made my stomach twist. “Michelle, that baggage is your son.”

A fresh wave of tears welled up, and I fought to keep silent, the weight of his words crashing down on me like a storm.

“I don’t want to be here anymore,” my mother’s voice cracked, breaking under the strain. “I don’t want to be your perfect, silent wife, and I definitely don’t want to raise your hellspawn any longer.”

The sound of drawers slamming—one after the other—made me flinch with each sharp bang. My chest tightened, fear crawling up my throat.

“What you do, and what you’ll turn that boy into…” she trailed off for a moment before her voice returned, louder, angrier, “I want no part of it.”

My father’s voice turned venomous, each word laced with a threat. “You walk out that door, and you don’t come crawling back. You’ll deserve everything you get, you ungrateful bitch.”

A suffocating silence followed. The air seemed to grow thick, heavy, and for a brief, agonizing moment, I dared to hope. But then I heard it—the front door creaking open, followed by the sound of it slamming shut so hard the walls seemed to tremble.

Something inside me snapped. I bolted from my hiding place, tears blurring my vision as I ran for the door, screaming, my voice raw and hoarse. “Mom! Mom!”

Before I could reach it, my father’s arm wrapped around my waist, yanking me back. I fought against him, my legs kicking, my arms flailing, desperate to break free. But he held me firm, his grip like iron. I screamed her name again, over and over, my throat burning, but my own voice felt foreign, like it belonged to someone else.

The front door stayed closed.

I prayed it was just a nightmare, that I’d wake up any second and everything would be okay. But the cold reality of my father’s grip, the emptiness that echoed through the house, told me otherwise.

I never woke up from that nightmare. And I never saw my mother again.

***

I gripped the edges of the sink until my knuckles went white, the cold porcelain biting into my palms. The faucet gushed as I splashed cold water on my face, the icy sting jolting my senses awake. When I looked up, my reflection stared back at me, haggard and haunted. Bloodshot eyes blinked under swollen lids, dark circles etched beneath them like bruises, a testament to nights spent wrestling with the same nightmare.

Third time this week.

I braced myself against the sink, my breath coming in slow, measured bursts. The nightmare never really left—it was always there, lingering just beneath the surface, waiting to drag me back to that night. No matter how many years passed, the shadows of that memory clung to me, heavy and unshakable, pulling me deeper into the world I’d been raised in.

I glanced at the clock on my nightstand, the glowing red digits cutting through the darkness. 5:30. Too late to try and sleep, too early to leave for the office. The silence in the room pressed in around me, thick and oppressive.

I needed to move, to shake off the weight of those memories. The floor was cool beneath my feet as I padded to the bathroom, turning on the shower without thinking. Hot water cascaded over me, steam rising in thick swirls, wrapping around my body like a shroud. The heat should have been comforting, but it couldn’t touch the cold ache sitting in my chest.

I leaned my forehead against the tile, letting the water stream down over my shoulders, soaking my hair. Each drop hit the floor with a steady rhythm, a distraction from the images still flashing behind my eyes—the slamming door, my mother’s voice, my father’s hand gripping me tightly. No matter how much time passed, I couldn’t wash it away. The past clung to me like damp clothes, heavy and suffocating.

With a deep sigh, I pushed off the wall and straightened up. There was work to do. Meetings. Deals. The performance of normalcy that kept everything in place. I could hear the steady hum of the city outside, slowly waking up, oblivious to the ghosts that lingered behind closed doors.

My father often commented that my being a part of the company we owned was a useless endeavor on my part, that I should let the people he put in place handle the business and that I needed to stay more out of the spotlight. He constantly felt the need to rule over my life with an iron fist, but my role in the construction company was the only thing in my life that I could control. The one thing he had no say in.

I tilted my head back and let the water cascade around me. The hot water was soothing, providing a temporary escape from the weight of my father’s expectations and the haunting memories of my past. As the steam filled the bathroom, I closed my eyes, trying to gather my thoughts and fortify myself for the day ahead.

My father never wasted an opportunity to remind me that my role in the company was pointless. “Let the people I put in charge handle things,” he’d say, his words sharp, dismissive. He always tried to control every aspect of my life with that iron grip of his. But the company—my part in it—was the one thing he couldn’t touch. It was the only space I had where his influence didn’t reach, where I could assert myself without him breathing down my neck.

I tilted my head back under the shower, letting the hot water pour over me. The heat soaked into my skin, loosening the tension knotted in my muscles. For a few moments, the weight of my father’s voice, the expectations, and the past drifted away in the swirling steam. The bathroom filled with it, a thick haze that momentarily blurred the edges of my thoughts.

The company was my sanctuary. In those blueprints, in the steady hum of construction sites and the satisfaction of projects completed, I found control. My father’s voice was a distant echo there, lost in the noise of progress. I knew every project by heart—every foundation, every steel beam. It was my domain, not his.

I exhaled slowly, turning off the water. The early morning light began to seep through the bathroom window, painting soft shadows on the tiles. I caught my reflection in the mirror—ice-blue eyes staring back at me, a mix of my mother’s ocean blue and my father’s steel gray. For a moment, I saw too much of him in that reflection. My jaw tightened, a vein ticking in my forehead. But I forced a deep breath, calming myself as I reached for the towel.

Wrapped in it, I padded into the bedroom, pulling on my black three-piece suit. The cool fabric settled against my skin, a protective layer between me and the world I was about to face.

The smell of fresh coffee greeted me as I entered the kitchen, its warmth already working to clear the lingering fog from my mind. I poured myself a cup and sank into one of the leather chairs, letting the heat seep into my fingers as I held the mug.

The silence of the penthouse pressed in around me, broken only by the distant hum of the city below. I rarely had visitors—just the maid who came twice a week and Sandy, when he wasn’t busy with business. The vastness of the space, though luxurious, felt hollow. Solitude clung to the corners, a constant, like the ticking of a clock.

I took a slow sip, savoring the warmth as it slid down my throat. The coffee was a brief comfort in the stillness, but it wasn’t enough to shake the sense of isolation that seemed to hang in the air. I finished the cup, setting it down with a quiet clink, and grabbed my keys from the counter. The cool metal rested reassuringly in my palm as I moved toward the door, the echo of my footsteps barely a whisper against the polished floor.

The penthouse, with all its sleek, pristine surfaces, often felt more like a gilded cage than a home. But as the door clicked shut behind me and I stepped into the hallway, a brief sense of freedom washed over me. I was ready to face the day ahead, the familiar pull of work beckoning me to the only place where I felt truly in control.

body.title: Lukas
body.content:
The building’s glass and steel exterior rose sharply against the soft dawn, casting cold reflections that mirrored the empire my family had meticulously crafted. As I pulled up to the security checkpoint, I lowered the window, and the brisk morning air washed over me, crisp and grounding. From outside, a faint ripple of laughter drifted in, surprising against the strict formality that usually hung over this place.

The guards were relaxed, exchanging a few easy jokes that broke the silence. For a fleeting second, their laughter cut through the polished emptiness surrounding me, reminding me of something I couldn’t quite grasp.

One of the guards, a solidly built man with lines of silver at his temples, stepped out of the booth, his stance easy and open—until his gaze landed on me. Recognition flickered, and in an instant, his relaxed posture stiffened, shoulders squared, the trace of a smile slipping into a curt, respectful nod.

“Good morning, Mr. Karpov,” he said, his tone steady but now stripped of the warmth he’d shown just seconds ago. He took my ID with mechanical precision, each movement efficient, practiced. Around him, the other guards snapped to attention, their casual ease replaced by rigid formality.

The shift was immediate, a silent acknowledgment of who I was—or rather, who they thought I was. It was a routine I’d seen countless times, yet each time, it hit the same. A reminder of the shadow that followed me, the reputation I’d inherited and could never quite outrun.

“Morning,” I replied, watching him slide my ID under the scanner, the faint beep punctuating the silence between us. We both knew it was unnecessary—there wasn’t a single person here who didn’t know my name or face. But in a place like this, appearances and formalities were the foundation, woven into every interaction.

He handed the card back with a brisk nod, his demeanor meticulously professional. “You’re all set, sir. Have a good day.”

I took the ID, pocketing it without a word. His eyes held a flicker of something—respect, maybe, or the guarded awareness people wore around me.

“Thank you,” I muttered, rolling up the window as the gate groaned open, the noise fading into the background as I drove past the checkpoint and into the parking lot. I pulled into my usual spot near the entrance, the closest I could get without attracting too much attention. For a moment, I sat there, fingers drumming absently on the steering wheel, eyes tracing the towering silhouette of the building.

It loomed above, all polished glass and steel, hiding a network of secrets in the shadows beyond those pristine walls. Out here, it looked like any other office complex, an architectural testament to success. But I knew better. Inside, under the sterile hum of fluorescent lights, the real work thrived in dim corridors, in coded conversations, in deals made off the books and off the radar. I took a deep breath, steeling myself for the day ahead, knowing I’d soon be stepping back into that world—a world that demanded as much from me as I’d ever taken from it.

Stepping out of the car, I tugged my jacket into place, running a hand over the fabric to smooth any creases—a habit drilled in from years of keeping up appearances. The sharp, rhythmic click of my shoes against the pavement broke through the morning’s stillness, each step echoing in the empty space around me. The air was crisp, carrying the faint scent of asphalt and steel, reminders of a city that never truly slept. As I neared the glass doors, my reflection stared back—composed, unreadable, the mask slipping into plaThe doors slid open with a soft whoosh, and a rush of cool, conditioned air greeted me as I stepped inside. The polished floors stretched out before me, gleaming under the stark, artificial lights, reflecting the pristine lines and calculated elegance of the lobby. The faint aroma of freshly brewed coffee drifted over from the café nestled to the side, a small comfort that was gone almost as soon as it reached me. As I moved deeper into the lobby, my path clear, I passed the security checkpoint without a glance from the guards. No one dared stop me here; my presence alone was an unspoken threat.

I kept my gaze fixed ahead, pretending not to notice the sudden hush that followed me through the lobby. Conversations cut off mid-sentence, laughter stopped short, lively chatter dissolving into tense murmurs.

It was the same every time—an unspoken ritual I’d grown used to, each pause and quieted word a reminder of the weight I brought with me. The air thickened whenever I entered, charged with a subtle deference I’d come to expect, yet it never failed to bring with it the same reminder.

The elevator doors slid open as I approached, and I stepped inside, the polished metal reflecting back an image I hardly recognized some days. The ride up was quick, and as I reached the executive level.

As I strode toward my office, the calm of the morning was interrupted by one of the employees stepping into my path. He was nervous, his hands shaking slightly as he extended a folder toward me. A brief glance upward revealed one of the HR staff, already sweating under the pressure of our encounter.

I raised an eyebrow, my annoyance clear. “What is this?” My tone was sharp, the unspoken reminder that wasting my time wasn’t an option.

The employee swallowed hard, his fingers trembling slightly as he adjusted his grip on the folder. “It’s the background check you requested, sir… on your new secretary.”

His nervousness did nothing to alleviate my irritation, though I took the folder from his hand, flipping it open without breaking stride. The details inside were expected—thorough, precise—but my mind was already on the meetings and the challenges ahead.

The weight of the day already felt suffocating as I stepped into my office, hoping for a moment of calm before the usual barrage of demands. But instead of the stillness I craved, I was greeted by an unexpected sight.

A figure was bent over my desk, her fingers moving quickly, rearranging my scattered papers with precision. The early morning sun streamed through the large windows, casting a warm glow over the room and illuminating her movements. Her focus was intense, her lips slightly pursed as she worked, unaware that I had entered.

“What exactly are you doing?” I asked, my voice cutting through the quiet, tinged with amusement.

She straightened up so fast that she nearly knocked over a stack of reports. Her cheeks flushed a delicate pink, her hands freezing midair like a child caught in the act. “Good morning, sir,” she stammered, blinking rapidly as if trying to reset herself. “I didn’t mean to barge in like this. I just saw that your desk was… well, a bit disorganized, and I thought I’d tidy it up for you. First impressions and all…” She trailed off, tucking a loose strand of hair behind her ear, her fingers trembling slightly.

I raised an eyebrow, taking in the sudden transformation of my workspace. My desk, usually a battlefield of scattered documents, now had a strange sense of order to it. The chaos I had grown used to was replaced with neatly stacked papers and organized files.

A rare sight.

“I appreciate the initiative,” I said, a slight edge of amusement softening my tone. “But next time, ask first.”

Her eyes widened, and she nodded quickly, almost too eagerly. “Of course, sir. It won’t happen again.” She straightened her blouse and adjusted her glasses, clearly trying to reassemble the professionalism she had lost in her flustered state.

Bemused, I watched her scramble to regain control, her movements fast, her nervous energy evident. She was trying to present herself as composed, but it was obvious she was still rattled. As I settled into the leather chair behind my now-neat desk, I allowed the moment to pass, shifting into the day ahead.

“Now, what’s on the schedule?” I asked, leaning back in my chair and crossing my arms, my tone sliding back into the sharper, more familiar edge of business.

She cleared her throat and quickly opened her notebook, her fingers flying over the pages. “You have a meeting first thing with the head of the Calido Group,” she said, handing me a neatly prepared folder.

I took it from her and flipped it open, the words barely registering before I let out a low, involuntary groan. The glossy images of the proposed nightclub stared back at me, accompanied by pages of overly optimistic financial projections. Ramirez Calido was always the same—he’d paint grandiose pictures of his ventures, all designed to dazzle investors, while hiding the true cost underneath layers of charm and deception.

The new secretary had enough tact to pretend she hadn’t heard my groan, though I noticed her lips twitch slightly as if she had to force herself not to react.

I scanned the documents, taking in the bold, slick presentation. The site was just a few blocks away from here, a prime location for a nightclub—if that was really all Calido wanted to build. My instincts told me otherwise. Beneath the polished facade, I could already sense the hidden angles, the shady side of the deal he wouldn’t dare put in writing.

I snapped the folder shut and sighed, the sound filled with the weight of yet another headache waiting to happen. “Wonderful,” I muttered under my breath.

The secretary shifted awkwardly on her feet, still standing by the desk, waiting for further instruction. I rubbed the bridge of my nose and closed my eyes for a brief second, trying to push the irritation away.

“Get me the numbers on his last project,” I said finally, leaning back and glancing at her. “And coffee. Strong.”

She nodded quickly, scribbling a note before hurrying out of the office. The soft click of the door closing behind her was the only sound left in the room. The sudden quiet brought no comfort—it was just a temporary pause before the day’s demands piled up again.

I sat there for a moment, staring at the closed folder, my fingers drumming lightly against the desk. The brief sense of peace I had hoped for had slipped away the moment I stepped into the building. The calm I craved, like always, was out of reach, drowned by the relentless noise of business.

He’d been circling my company like a vulture for months, desperate to have us back his latest endeavor. We both knew what it really was—a thinly veiled front for his illegal operations, just like all the others. This time, he was offering a forty percent share in the profits, as if that would make his underhanded dealings more palatable.

The sheer audacity of his demands was exhausting. Each proposal he sent my way was more absurd than the last, filled with grand promises and vague threats that did nothing to shake my resolve. His arrogance, while infuriating, was nothing new. I’d learned long ago that showing my frustration would only give him more satisfaction.

I glanced up at the secretary, standing there with her clipboard and an air of quiet professionalism. “When is this meeting?”

My voice remained steady, but there was no hiding the tension threading through each word. She flipped through one of the folders in her arms, then checked her watch. “In fifteen minutes, sir.”

Her tone was composed, though I caught a flicker of sympathy in her eyes. Everyone knew dealing with Ramirez Calido was like trying to wrestle a snake without getting bitten.

I sighed, glaring down at the folder one last time before standing up and making my way to the conference room. The weight of another round of negotiations with Calido sat heavily on my shoulders, pressing down as I walked through the quiet hallways. My footsteps echoed off the polished marble floors, each one a reminder of the confrontation to come.

When I stepped into the conference room, Calido was already there, lounging in his chair like he owned the place. His bright, cocky smile flashed across the room the moment he saw me. The tailored lines of his expensive suit and the casual way he leaned back spoke volumes. He was confident—no, overconfident, like always.

“Well, if it isn’t the mini-boss,” he sneered, his voice dripping with mockery. “Have you finally decided my proposal is good enough for the Karpov empire?”

His words hung in the air like a taunt, the smirk on his face practically daring me to rise to the bait. I knew better. Ramirez loved pushing buttons, testing limits, seeing how far he could go before getting a reaction.

I took a slow, measured breath, sinking into the chair across from him, forcing myself to remain calm. This was going to be a long exchange, and I’d need every ounce of patience I had to get through it. His arrogance filled the room, and I could already tell he had no intention of making this easy.

***

After nearly three grueling hours of verbal sparring with Calido, I finally managed to escape back to my office, my body and mind drained from the exhausting negotiations. While I’d succeeded in pushing through some of my demands and tempering his, the smug satisfaction on his face as he left the conference room lingered in my thoughts, gnawing at me. Calido had walked away thinking he had the upper hand, and that alone made the deal feel like a pyrrhic victory.

I leaned back in my chair, staring at the piles of reports that awaited me, their edges spilling over the desk like an avalanche of obligations. The once neatly arranged papers, courtesy of my new secretary, had reverted back to chaos, each document screaming for attention. The thought of diving into monthly reports after the marathon with Calido made my head pound, a dull throb already spreading behind my eyes.

This wasn’t where I should have been. My focus needed to be on cleaning up the mess Carpathia had left in his wake. His latest project had spiraled into disaster, and now the fallout was mine to manage—more collateral damage that my father would, no doubt, be eager to remind me was my responsibility. I rubbed my temples, feeling the weight of it all pressing down harder.

I reached for the damage report, flipping it open without much thought, but the numbers hit me like a punch to the gut. My fingers tightened around the paper, and I could feel my pulse rising, the thudding in my temples intensifying.

“You’ve got to be fucking kidding me!” The words burst out, sharp and bitter, as I scanned the figures. The damage was far worse than I’d imagined—staggering losses that would cripple some of our operations if not addressed immediately. I tossed the report back on the desk, my frustration flaring hotter as the implications sank in.

Millions lost. Equipment destroyed. And the delays—the delays alone would set us back months. Every page of the report was a fresh blow, each figure another reminder that the cleanup wasn’t just a logistical nightmare, but a ticking time bomb.

I slammed my fist onto the desktop, the force rattling the papers, pens, and everything else cluttering the surface. The impact reverberated through my arm, but the frustration inside me barely lessened. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw my secretary jump at the sudden noise. Her eyes widened, and I caught a glimpse of alarm flicker across her face as she stood frozen, uncertain.

I ignored her and glared down at the chaotic stack of papers, my mind racing. Loose ends—missing pages, incomplete reports, careless work. It infuriated me. I hated having to clean up after people who couldn’t be bothered to do their jobs properly, especially when I was already juggling more than enough. My father had taught me to value control above all else, and seeing things fall apart like this was intolerable.

With a sharp exhale, I stood up, feeling the heat of my anger rising. One last look at the pile of papers—the latest burden thrown onto an already overwhelming day—sent a surge of frustration through me. Before I could think, I grabbed the stack and hurled it across the room. The pages fluttered wildly before scattering across the floor, a disorganized mess reflecting the storm inside me.

Helplessness hit me like a wave, sharp and bitter. It wasn’t a feeling I was used to, and I hated it. It reminded me of what had happened a few days ago, of the mess Carpathia had created. He knew how to get under my skin, how to play the game better than most. Worse, he seemed to know exactly which buttons to press, and I couldn’t stand the thought of losing control, of being a pawn in whatever sick game he was playing.

The thought gnawed at me, twisting in my gut, making my hands tremble slightly at my sides.

“Sir?” a cautious voice cut through the fog of my thoughts, pulling me back into the present. I turned, my eyes narrowing as they landed on my secretary—what was her name again? Lydia? Lisa? I couldn’t remember. She stood at the edge of the room, her gaze flickering from me to the scattered papers on the floor, then back again. She shifted nervously, her hands clasped together, clearly unsure how to approach me in this state.

“What do you want?” I snapped, the frustration spilling over without restraint. The last thing I needed right now was another interruption. Another demand for my time, for my attention. My patience was hanging by a thread, and every new intrusion felt like another weight, dragging me down.

She looked briefly startled by the venom in my tone, but to her credit, she recovered quickly, straightening her posture with a nervous swallow. “Um, Mr. Artem Karpov is on line one for you,” she said, her voice wavering slightly but still maintaining a veneer of professionalism.

My scowl deepened, an involuntary reaction at the mention of his name. The last person I wanted to hear from right now was my father. Just the thought of him made my blood pressure spike. I toyed with the idea of ignoring the call, letting it go unanswered, but I knew better. Dismissing him would only invite more trouble later, and the tongue-lashing I’d receive at home was something I couldn’t afford right now—not on top of everything else. His constant anger was a shadow over my life, always lurking, always ready to smother me at the slightest misstep.

With an irritated wave of my hand, I dismissed the secretary. As soon as the door clicked shut behind her, I snatched the office phone, jabbing the button for line one. “Father.” My greeting was clipped, any hint of respect carefully stripped from my voice.

Our relationship had been strained for years, and the tension had only worsened in recent months. Every call, every conversation felt like a battleground, each word loaded with the potential to spark another argument. His overbearing nature and relentless interference were the main sources of my frustration, the reasons I felt trapped under his thumb, even in my own office.

“Lukas, turn on the news. Right now,” he barked, skipping any semblance of pleasantries. His voice carried the familiar harshness of a command, laden with the authority he wielded so effortlessly, and it struck the same defensive chord in me that it always did.

I clenched my jaw, glaring at the remote sitting on my desk. The 72-inch screen on the wall loomed over me, a silent reminder of the constant surveillance I felt under my father’s gaze, whether he was physically present or not.

“Why?” I shot back, unable to resist the small act of rebellion. I knew it would piss him off. My father hated being questioned, and the rebellious streak in me, the part of me that resented his control, relished these small moments of defiance.

“You’ll see,” he snapped, his tone brimming with impatience. I could hear the barely concealed annoyance seeping through the phone, and I smirked inwardly, knowing I’d gotten under his skin. His voice always had that edge, a mix of impatience and frustration that never failed to drag me back to my childhood, to the days of endless pressure and expectations I could never quite meet.

It had shaped me—this constant battle between us—but he would never understand the weight of it. He only saw what I wasn’t, what I should have been by now.

I bit back the snarky reply sitting on the tip of my tongue. It would have been satisfying to push him further, to see how much I could rile him up, but I knew the repercussions that would follow. I’d dealt with them plenty of times before, but right now, with Carpathia breathing down my neck and the pressure building on every front, I didn’t need my father’s wrath on top of it all.

As I flicked on the news, a bitter taste rose in my throat. The TV came to life with a flicker of light, and for a moment, I hesitated. It was always the same—an order barked through the phone like I was a dog he could command at will.

But then the image on the screen came into focus, and I felt the familiar knot of dread tightening in my stomach. I barely stopped the groan from escaping, keeping my face impassive despite the urge to curse aloud. My father thrived on pulling the strings, waiting for me to jump whenever he snapped his fingers.

A reporter stood outside a warehouse that I knew too well. Her face was composed, but I saw the cracks beneath the surface—the slight crease in her brow, the tension in the way she tugged her hair behind her ear, as though every word she spoke was a battle to remain composed. Behind her, the scene was a chaotic mess of flashing lights, cop cars, and forensic vans, their lights painting the warehouse in harsh reds and blues. Officers moved with a grim purpose, combing through the wreckage. My stomach churned.

The warehouse wasn’t just any building—it was one of ours. A vital hub in our logistics network, and the fact that the police were swarming all over it like flies made the situation far more dangerous than I wanted to admit. The reporter’s voice carried an edge of urgency beneath her professionalism, every syllable adding weight to the disaster unfolding in front of me.

“Last evening, authorities were alerted to this location after an anonymous tip-off. Details are scarce, but it appears there was a confrontation between two notorious gangs, the Serpent Kings and the Chain Vultures, just hours before police arrived.”

The camera panned over the scene: shattered windows, scorch marks licking the walls, debris scattered across the lot like the remnants of a war zone. Police officers sifted through the wreckage, their movements methodical and heavy with the weight of yet another crime scene to process.

I clenched my jaw, eyes narrowing at the footage. I knew where this was headed. The inevitable responsibility would fall on me like it always did, but I still had to ask, if only to delay the moment. “What about it?” I asked, forcing my voice to stay neutral even as tension coiled tighter inside me.

“This has gone too far,” my father snapped, his voice sharp, biting. “Fix it.”

Of course. Fix it. As though that was all it took to erase whatever mess Carpathia had stirred up. My fists curled into tight balls at my sides. “Why do I have to fix it?” The frustration bubbled up, slipping through my control. “Carpathia’s the one behind all of this, and yet I’m the one—”

“Lukas.” My father’s voice sliced through my words like a knife, cold and dismissive. “You will fix this. If you plan on ever running the business—on ever being worthy of being called my son.”

The line went dead with a click, the dial tone blaring in my ear before I realized he’d hung up. His words were still ringing in my head, the sting of them sharper than I cared to admit. I slammed the phone down into the cradle, the force of it rattling the desk as I muttered through clenched teeth.

“Un-fucking-believable.”

I stared at the phone, the anger boiling beneath the surface, every muscle in my body tight with tension. Of course, he would dump his dirty work on me again. Of course, he’d expect me to clean up this disaster without hesitation.

I pushed myself away from the desk, my movements sharp, barely controlled as I paced across the office. My hands dragged through my hair, pulling at the strands in frustration. The walls felt like they were closing in, my thoughts racing with no clear direction. With every step, the weight of his expectations bore down on me, pressing harder and harder.

In a burst of frustration, I kicked the trash bin next to my desk. It spun across the floor, scattering its contents and leaving my office even more disheveled. The mess on the floor mirrored the mess in my head. The room felt smaller, more suffocating with each passing second. Control—something I thrived on—was slipping further from my grasp.

I took a deep breath, fighting to keep my temper in check. The urge to punch something, to let the rage boil over, was almost overwhelming. Damn it. How does he expect me to fix this? It wasn’t my fault that Carpathia had thrown everything into chaos, but somehow, my father always managed to shove the fallout into my lap. Always.

Shaking my head, I stalked over to the floor-to-ceiling window that overlooked Brooklyn’s business district, the city sprawling beneath me in neat grids. I leaned one arm against the glass, pressing my forehead against the cool surface as I let out another long, frustrated sigh. The city buzzed with life below, oblivious to the storm brewing in my world, the chaos that Carpathia had unleashed.

He wanted this—wanted his rivals to crack, to slip into disarray. And damn it, so far, he was getting exactly what he wanted. The more chaos he stirred, the easier it became for him to tighten his grip. I’d been helpless to stop him so far, and that burned worse than anything.

But that had to change.

I pushed the anger down, burying it beneath the cold calculation I knew I needed right now. This was going to take everything I had—every favor I could pull, every ounce of leverage I could muster. I would need to control the narrative, manipulate the media, and keep our name from getting dragged through the mud. Failure wasn’t an option. Not if I wanted to prove myself—to my father, to myself.

I pulled away from the window, reaching into my pocket and pulling out one of the burner phones I kept on hand. The familiar weight of it in my palm was a strange comfort amid the chaos, a reminder that I wasn’t entirely powerless here. The number I dialed was one I knew by heart, each press of the buttons almost automatic.

It rang once before a voice picked up, low and steady. I didn’t wait for pleasantries.

“Sandy, I need you to send someone to do a deep clean,” I said, letting my Russian accent slip through, thickening each word. Old habits. You never knew who might be listening. The code phrase had been used before, and Sandy wouldn’t need any more explanation.

The line went quiet for a beat, long enough that I wondered if Sandy hadn’t heard me. Then, his voice cut through, laced with a familiar hint of exasperation. “I’m guessing you got a call from daddy dearest. Who needs to be dealt with this time, and why?” He knew the routine all too well.

I let out a slow breath, my gaze drifting back to the television, where the warehouse footage still dominated the screen—police officers, crime scene tape, and evidence bags. It was a mess, and it was my mess to clean up, courtesy of my father’s grand expectations. “You didn’t catch the news?” I asked, my tone dry. “Looks like our visit to the warehouse attracted some unwanted attention.”

“Nah,” Sandy replied with a dismissive snort, though I could hear the concern edging into his voice. “You know I don’t watch that depressing shit. It’s too much.”

I chuckled under my breath. Of course, Sandy would try to brush it off with humor, even now. “Well, it’s all over the news. Seems like the boys in blue got curious about our little warehouse escapade.”

The line went silent for a moment before I heard Sandy let out a long, resigned sigh. “Alright, who needs the money? The Boys in Blue? The media? Or those who sit on the judgment seats?” His tone shifted, all business now, ready to mobilize the resources we’d need to put out this fire.

I smirked, though it barely reached my eyes. “All of the above, apparently.” I ran a hand through my hair, the weight of it all pressing heavier by the second. “My father’s convinced I have to fix this.” My voice held more frustration than I intended, the words tasting bitter on my tongue.

Sandy chuckled, the dry sound on the other end of the line. “Of course he is. That’s the price you pay when the King of Brooklyn is your old man.”

“Self-proclaimed king,” I muttered automatically. It didn’t matter if it was true—if he was the king. To me, he was nothing more than a figurehead with an iron grip on my life, leaving me to do all the dirty work behind the scenes. The bitterness in my voice was unmistakable, even to me.

Sandy was quiet for a moment, and when he spoke again, his voice was more serious. “You want this mess to go away, right? Not for him—but for your own plans.” He understood the stakes, the long game I was trying to play. This wasn’t just about damage control. This was about my future, about stepping out of my father’s oppressive shadow once and for all.

“Exactly,” I said, my voice tired but firm. I leaned back against the glass, the cool surface grounding me. “I’m not doing this to clean up his messes anymore. This merger is supposed to be my ticket. I’m done playing the janitor in his empire.”

“You can make a lot of things disappear with a few thousand bucks.” Sandy’s voice was steady, reassuring in the way only he could be. “Leave it to me. We’ll take care of it.”

“I hope so,” I muttered, running a hand down my face. “This is the third time this month we’ve had to pay them off.” The incidents were happening too often, and each one chipped away at my patience.

“Money’s never been a problem for you,” Sandy replied almost cheerfully. “We’ve got it covered. You just focus on your wedding—oops, I mean your merger.” The line went dead before I could respond, leaving me alone with his parting jab hanging in the air.

For a moment, I wasn’t sure whether I wanted to laugh or curse him out. Sandy’s flippant attitude, while usually a welcome distraction, felt sharper today, like a reminder of just how much pressure was bearing down on me.

I slipped the burner phone back into my pocket and leaned my forehead against the window, the cool glass fogging slightly as I exhaled. My breath left small, clouded patches on the pane as I stared out at the city below. Brooklyn stretched out before me, vast and indifferent.

This merger—this wedding—was supposed to be my way out, my chance to finally prove myself without my father’s shadow looming over every move I made. But every day, it felt like that shadow grew heavier, more suffocating. I pressed my fist against the glass, jaw tight.

Failure wasn’t an option. Not this time.

This was my chance, and I’d be damned if I didn’t reap every single benefit it promised.

body.title: Jayna
body.content:
I stood in the center of the bustling room, my hands resting on my hips as I watched the workers meticulously drape the soft, flowing fabric across the stage. The material billowed gently, catching the light as it created a cascading, elegant backdrop for the event. Around me, the steady clink of cutlery and the rustling of linens filled the air, blending with the hum of quiet conversations and the occasional burst of laughter from the crew. The space buzzed with a mix of concentration and anticipation, each person intent on their task.

In the corner, the rolled-up banner for Angela’s Angel Foundation in partnership with Sheltered Kids waited to be unveiled. Its bold, vibrant lettering promised hope and change, a visual testament to all the work that had gone into this moment. The bright colors and uplifting message felt like a beacon, a reminder of what we were here to accomplish. The transformation of the space, from an empty hall to a room brimming with potential, made me smile.

I took in the scene, my heart swelling with pride. This wasn’t just another event—this was special. It was a tribute to my mother’s legacy, something she would have been so proud to see. The foundation’s work meant the world to her, and today, as we prepared to make a real impact on the lives of these kids, I felt her presence more than ever. It was as if, through every draped piece of fabric and polished table setting, her influence lingered.

I was pulled from my thoughts by the sound of someone clearing their throat. Turning, I saw Wanda and Lauren approaching. Wanda, with her calm, steady presence, always brought a sense of order to the chaos, while Lauren’s bright energy was like a spark that kept everything moving.

“Jayna, everything is coming along wonderfully,” Wanda said, her voice reassuring, as it always was.

I smiled, feeling the weight of her words settle over me like a balm. “Thanks, Wanda. I’m really pleased with how it’s turning out,” I said, my gratitude for her and the team overflowing.

Lauren stepped forward, holding a clipboard close to her chest. “We just need your approval on the final schedule and a quick walk through of the setup,” she said, her excitement evident even in her professional tone.

I took the clipboard from her, scanning the well-organized schedule with a sense of quiet satisfaction.
